plain_explanation: Checks whether values consistently move up or down over time, without assuming they follow a straight line.
example: Mann-Kendall p = 0.02 → The upward pattern is unlikely to be caused by random variation alone.

plain_explanation: A robust estimate of the rate of change that is less affected by unusual values or outliers than a simple average line.
example: Theil-Sen slope = +1.2 mm/month per year → Rainfall is rising by about 1.2 mm each year, and this estimate is resistant to one-off extreme months.

plain_explanation: The average straight-line rate of change over the entire period. It finds the best-fit line through all the data points.
example: OLS slope = −0.5 °C per decade → On average, temperature dropped by 0.5 degrees every ten years.

plain_explanation: A likely range for the true rate of change. If this range does not include zero, we can be fairly confident the change is real (not just noise).
example: 95% CI: [+0.3, +2.1] mm/month/year → The real trend is very likely somewhere between +0.3 and +2.1.

plain_explanation: The probability of seeing a trend this strong if there were no real trend at all — just random noise. A small p-value (below 0.05) means the trend is unlikely to be a coincidence.
example: p = 0.01 → There is only a 1% chance that random variation alone would produce a pattern this strong.

plain_explanation: The observed trend is unlikely to be due to chance alone. Here we use a threshold of p < 0.05, meaning less than a 5% chance the trend is random noise.
example: "Significant at the 95% confidence level" → We are 95% confident the trend is real, not just luck.

plain_explanation: The value after the usual seasonal pattern is removed. For example, subtracting the average July rainfall from this July's rainfall shows whether this July was unusually wet or dry.
example: July 2023 anomaly = +15 mm → It rained 15 mm more than the long-term July average.

plain_explanation: Nearby months tend to be similar to each other (a wet June often leads to a wet July). This can make a trend look more certain than it really is, so we check for it and warn you.
example: Lag-1 autocorrelation = 0.45 → There is moderate month-to-month similarity; the p-value may be overly optimistic.

plain_explanation: A change that runs in a consistent direction over time — values generally going up, or generally going down, across months or years.
example: An upward trend in AOD means haze levels have generally been rising over the analysis period.

plain_explanation: A list of measurements of the same thing (like rainfall) for the same place, ordered by date — month by month or year by year.
example: Monthly rainfall for Lahore from January 2000 to December 2024 is a time series with 300 data points.

plain_explanation: The range of years used to calculate the 'normal' or 'average' value for each month. Anomalies are measured as deviations from this baseline.
example: Baseline 2001–2020 means the average for each calendar month is computed from those 20 years.

plain_explanation: When averaging satellite data over a region, each grid cell's value is weighted by its area. Cells near the equator are larger than cells near the poles, so this gives a fairer average.
example: A 1° cell at 25°N covers more area than a 1° cell at 35°N, so it gets more weight in the regional average.

plain_explanation: A model-based reconstruction of past weather and climate conditions. It blends many types of observations (satellites, weather stations, balloons) into a consistent global picture. It is not a direct measurement.
example: MERRA-2 temperature is a reanalysis product — it fills gaps between weather stations using physics-based models.

plain_explanation: A measure of how much haze, dust, smoke, or pollution is in the atmosphere. Higher AOD means more particles blocking sunlight.
example: AOD = 0.8 means the atmosphere is fairly hazy; AOD = 0.1 means relatively clear skies.
